scenes.title: Poseidon Crosses the Sea
scenes.summary: Having brought Hector and the Trojans to the ships, Zeus turns his shining eyes away to the lands of the Thracians and the Mysians, the mare-milkers who live on milk and the Abii, most just of men, sure that no immortal will help either side. But Poseidon is watching from the peak of Thracian Samos, where Ida, Troy and the ships can all be seen; he pities the Achaeans and is fiercely indignant with Zeus. In four strides he reaches his golden house at Aegae, yokes his bronze-footed horses, and drives over the waves while the sea beasts frolic around their lord and the sea parts for joy. He leaves the horses in a cave between Tenedos and Imbros, with ambrosial fodder and golden hobbles, and goes to the Achaean army.

scenes.title: Poseidon and the Two Ajaxes
scenes.summary: The Trojans follow Hector like a flame or a storm wind, hoping to take the ships. Poseidon, in the likeness of Calchas, tells the two Ajaxes that the Achaeans can hold the Trojans everywhere except where Hector, who claims to be the son of Zeus, leads them like a flame, and that the two of them must stand firm and rouse the rest. He strikes them with his staff, fills them with might, makes their limbs light, and darts away like a hawk. The son of Oileus knows the god from behind as he goes, for gods are easy to know, and both men feel their hands and feet quivering for battle.

scenes.title: The Close Ranks
scenes.summary: Poseidon goes to the men in the rear, worn out and weeping at the sight of the Trojans over the wall, and urges on Teucer, Leitus, Peneleos, Thoas, Deipyrus, Meriones and Antilochus. Their slackness is a shame, he says: the Trojans, who used to be like timid deer, now fight at the ships through their leader's fault and the army's slackness; even if Agamemnon is truly to blame for dishonoring Achilles, they must not hold back from war, for the hearts of good men can be healed. The battalions form around the two Ajaxes, so close that shield presses on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man, and the horsehair crests touch when the men nod.

scenes.title: Hector Is Checked
scenes.summary: Hector leads the Trojans on like a boulder that a winter torrent breaks loose from a crest, bounding down until it reaches level ground. He threatens to sweep through the huts and ships to the sea, but at the close-packed battalions he is stopped, pushed back by swords and spears, and gives ground, reeling. He calls on the Trojans, Lycians and Dardanians to stand by him, sure that the husband of Hera has roused him. Deiphobus comes forward behind his shield; Meriones' spear strikes it and snaps at the socket, and Meriones goes back to his hut for another.

scenes.title: Imbrius and Amphimachus
scenes.summary: Teucer kills Imbrius, son of Mentor, who had married Medesicaste, a bastard daughter of Priam, and lived in Priam's house; he falls like an ash tree felled on a mountain peak. Hector throws at Teucer, misses, and kills Amphimachus, son of Cteatus; when he tries to take the helmet, Ajax's spear on his shield boss drives him back from both bodies. Stichius and Menestheus carry Amphimachus to the Achaeans, and the two Ajaxes carry off Imbrius like two lions with a goat snatched from the dogs; the son of Oileus cuts off his head in anger for Amphimachus and sends it rolling like a ball to Hector's feet.

scenes.title: Poseidon Rouses Idomeneus
scenes.summary: Angry for his grandson Amphimachus, Poseidon goes along the huts and ships. Idomeneus, coming from a companion wounded behind the knee, meets him in the likeness of Thoas, who asks where the Achaeans' threats have gone. Idomeneus answers that no man is to blame: it must be the pleasure of Zeus that the Achaeans perish here, nameless, far from Argos. Poseidon wishes that whoever holds back today may become a plaything for dogs and tells him to arm, for even poor men's prowess counts when it is joined. Idomeneus arms and goes out like the lightning that Zeus brandishes from Olympus.

scenes.title: Idomeneus and Meriones
scenes.summary: Near the hut Idomeneus meets Meriones, who has come for a spear, and asks whether he is wounded or brings a message. Meriones has broken his spear on Deiphobus' shield; Idomeneus has twenty Trojan spears in his hut, taken from men he has killed, and Meriones answers that he too has Trojan spoils, though they are far off, and fights among the foremost. Idomeneus knows his prowess: in an ambush, where the coward changes color and his teeth chatter while the brave man prays for the fight, no one could fault him, and any wound he took would be in front. Meriones takes a spear, and the two go out like Ares and his son Rout; since the two Ajaxes and Teucer guard the middle of the ships against Hector, Idomeneus chooses the left.

scenes.title: The Rope of War
scenes.summary: When the Trojans see Idomeneus blazing like a flame, they come at him, and the battle closes like a storm raising dust on the roads, bristling with spears and blinding with the glare of bronze. Zeus wants victory for Hector and the Trojans to glorify Achilles, though he does not want the Achaean army destroyed; Poseidon, of the same parentage but younger, helps the Achaeans secretly, in the likeness of a man. Between them the two brothers stretch the rope of strife and war over both armies, unbreakable and not to be loosed, and it loosens the knees of many.

scenes.title: Othryoneus and Asius
scenes.summary: Half-gray as he is, Idomeneus leaps among the Trojans and routs them. He kills Othryoneus of Cabesus, who had been promised Cassandra without bride-price if he drove the Achaeans from Troy, and mocks him with an offer of Agamemnon's fairest daughter if he will help sack Ilios. Asius comes to the rescue on foot in front of his horses, and Idomeneus spears him in the throat; he falls like an oak or a pine felled for ship-timber and lies roaring, clutching the bloody dust. Antilochus kills his stunned charioteer and drives the horses off to the Achaeans.

scenes.title: Hypsenor and Alcathous
scenes.summary: Deiphobus throws at Idomeneus, who crouches under his round shield; the spear strikes down Hypsenor instead, and Deiphobus boasts that Asius now has an escort to the house of Hades. Antilochus covers Hypsenor with his shield, and Mecisteus and Alastor carry him to the ships. Idomeneus kills Alcathous, Anchises' son-in-law and husband of Hippodameia, whom Poseidon bewitches and binds so that he stands like a pillar; the spear fixed in his heart quivers with its beating. Idomeneus asks Deiphobus whether three dead for one is a fair exchange, and tells his descent from Zeus through Minos and Deucalion.

scenes.title: Aeneas Comes to the Fight
scenes.summary: Deiphobus goes for Aeneas, who stands at the edge of the throng nursing his wrath against Priam, and asks him to defend Alcathous, who reared him. Idomeneus awaits him like a boar at bay and calls his companions; Aeneas calls Deiphobus, Paris and Agenor, and the army follows him like sheep after a ram. Aeneas' spear misses; Idomeneus kills Oenomaus, but his legs are no longer quick, and he gives ground step by step. Deiphobus throws at him again and kills Ascalaphus, son of Ares, who sits on Olympus not knowing, held back by the will of Zeus. As Deiphobus takes Ascalaphus' helmet, Meriones spears him in the arm, and Polites leads him to his chariot.

scenes.title: Antilochus under Poseidon's Guard
scenes.summary: Aeneas kills Aphareus; Antilochus kills Thoon and strips him, turning among the enemy with his spear always moving, while Poseidon keeps every weapon from him. Adamas' spear breaks in Antilochus' shield, made powerless by Poseidon, and as Adamas draws back Meriones spears him between the genitals and the navel, where Ares is most painful for mortals; he writhes around the spear like a roped ox until Meriones pulls it out.

scenes.title: Menelaus, Helenus and Peisander
scenes.summary: Helenus kills Deipyrus with a great Thracian sword. Menelaus goes at Helenus, and the two strike at once: Helenus' arrow bounces off Menelaus' corselet like beans from a winnowing shovel, and Menelaus' spear pins Helenus' hand to his bow; Agenor binds it with a sling. Peisander, led by an evil fate, breaks his spear on Menelaus' shield and swings an axe at his helmet; Menelaus strikes him on the forehead and kills him, and over the body he denounces the Trojans, who carried off his wife without fear of Zeus, god of guests, and never have their fill of war.

scenes.title: Harpalion and Euchenor
scenes.summary: Harpalion, son of Pylaemenes, stabs Menelaus' shield and draws back; Meriones' arrow kills him, and the Paphlagonians carry him to Ilios with his father following in tears. In anger for his guest-friend, Paris shoots Euchenor of Corinth, son of the seer Polyidus, who had told him that he would die of a grievous sickness at home or be killed among the ships at Troy; he had chosen Troy.

scenes.title: The Two Ajaxes Hold Hector
scenes.summary: Hector does not know that his men are being cut down on the left of the ships. He holds on where he first broke through the gates and the wall, at the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus, where the wall is lowest; there the Boeotians, Ionians, Locrians, Phthians and Epeians hold him off, with the picked Athenians under Menestheus and the Phthians under Medon and Podarces. The two Ajaxes stand side by side like two oxen pulling a plow. Telamonian Ajax's companions take his shield when he tires; the Locrians, who carry bows and slings rather than helmets, shields and spears, shoot from behind and break the Trojan ranks.

scenes.title: Polydamas' Counsel at the Ships
scenes.summary: The Trojans would have been driven back to Ilios had not Polydamas told Hector that the gods give one man war, another dancing or song, another a good mind, and urged him to call the best men together and decide whether to fall on the ships or withdraw unharmed: he fears that the Achaeans will repay yesterday's debt, while a man insatiable of war waits by the ships. Hector agrees, leaps from his chariot, and goes to give his orders.

scenes.title: Hector Rebukes Paris
scenes.summary: Hector goes through the Trojans like a snowy mountain, looking for Deiphobus, Helenus, Adamas and Asius, and finds them dead or wounded. On the left he finds Paris and reproaches him; Paris answers that he has fought without rest, that Deiphobus and Helenus have gone away wounded in the hand, and that he will follow. They go where the fighting is thickest, among Cebriones, Polydamas and the Ascanians who had come the morning before, and the Trojans come on like waves driven by a storm, with Hector in front, testing the Achaean ranks behind his shield; but he does not shake them.

scenes.title: Ajax Challenges Hector
scenes.summary: Ajax strides out and tells Hector that the Achaeans have been beaten by the lash of Zeus, not for lack of skill, and that Hector will soon pray for horses swifter than hawks to carry him back to the city. An eagle flies high on the right, and the Achaeans shout at the omen. Hector calls Ajax a blundering braggart and swears that he will die at the ships and glut the dogs and birds of the Trojans. The two armies shout against each other, and the roar reaches the upper air and the rays of Zeus.

days.label: Day 26
days.note: The third day of battle continues (11.1 to 18.242). Book 13 follows the fighting at the ships from the moment Hector breaks in to Ajax's challenge, while Zeus looks away and Poseidon secretly rallies the Achaeans. The battle goes on into Book 14, where Nestor hears the din from his hut (14.1).
